newsitem.title: USA: Away on business - Green hotels.
newsitem.headline: Away on business - Green hotels.

text.p: Travelers are increasingly being asked to help hotels and motels do a favour for the environment, and the appeal seems to be working.

In the four or so months since a lodging industry trade association began offering laminated cards advising guests that they can re-use their sheets and towels, about a half million of the notices have been distributed to properties for placement in guest rooms around the country.
"We are continuing to see an increase in interest" in the project, said a spokeswoman for the American Hotel and Motel Association, which is selling the cards to its member properties.
Printed in five languages, the cards are designed to cut down on the trips hotel linens make to the laundry room -- and with that reduce a major source of energy and water consumption.

Compliance is voluntary. A guest who places the card on his or her pillow will find a change of bed linens every three days or so, instead of nightly. Only towels tossed on the floor or left in the tub will be replaced.

Holiday Inn Worldwide launched a similar sheet and towel programme in 1994 that has now spread to 650 out of more than 2,000 properties, and "the number is growing weekly," said spokesman Craig Smith.

"We've had no guest complaints whatsover," he said. "A few have asked questions, but it seems to be a good way to teach people that we can all do our part. Frankly we don't wash our sheets every night at home anyway."

Smith said Holiday Inn estimates its programme is saving just under 4 million gallons of water each month and preventing about 26,000 gallons of cleaning solution from being released into the environment every month.
The hotel-motel trade group reports varying levels of compliance as far as guests are concerned.

A recent check with managers of Amelia Island Plantation in Florida showed as many as 30 percent of the guests were opting to re-use towels. The facility reported positive feedback from guests, the association said.

In recent years many segments of the lodging industry have become more environmentally conscious, often in ways invisible to guests. Some have found ways to recycle restaurant leftovers into livestock feed; others are using low-volume shower heads or energy-saving lights and different approaches to heating and cooling.
The Houston-based "Green" Hotels Association, which provides properties with guidelines to make them environmentally friendly, says 100 institutions worldwide have become charter members.
"We find guests are so enthusiastic and the comment cards they turn in reflect that. One manager said no matter what he does, they want more."
The association provides a free checklist for meeting planners to send to a hotel in advance to find out how "green" a property is.
It can be obtained through the association's e-mail address: green(at)greenhotels.com

Business travelers: Question, complaint or pet peeve? Send them to Away on Business, c/o Reuters, Room 1170, 311 S. Wacker Dr., Chicago 60606.
